title: SYSK Selects: Why isn't the U.S. on the metric system?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun episode asking why the United States has not fully adopted the metric system. The hosts trace the history of measurement from body-part units to the French metric system devised by Gabriel Mouton (1670) and adopted during the French Revolution, Napoleon's spread of the meter, Thomas Jefferson's early US standards effort, the snub of the US from the 1875 Treaty of the Meter, Andrew Johnson's 1866 law legalizing metric use, Mendenhall's 1893 order tying US units to metric standards, the 1960 redefinition into SI, and the 1975 Metric Conversion Act with its voluntary transition. They note that the US customary system is still used, that metric is widespread in industry, science, and everyday products, and cite the Mars Climate Orbiter loss from mixed units. A closing listener mail segment features a listener from Anchorage, Alaska, who is preparing for a Rotary exchange year abroad.
rerun_of: Why isn't the U.S. on the metric system?

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to metric question
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode and the hosts banter about recording setup. They frame the topic: the US is the only industrialized nation not fully on the metric system, though it is widely used.

segments.title: Origins of body-part and customary units
segments.summary: The hosts describe early units based on body parts such as the thumb, foot, and forearm, and the acre as the land a team of oxen could plow in a day. They note the customary system is unscientific and that standardization became necessary as societies and trade grew.

segments.title: Gabriel Mouton and the French metric system
segments.summary: France's attempts to standardize measurements led to the French Revolution and the National Assembly. Gabriel Mouton's 1670 base-ten proposal, tied to the Earth's circumference, was adopted, and a commission set three principles for the system.

segments.title: Defining the meter and Napoleon's spread
segments.summary: The meter was defined as one ten-millionth of the meridian quadrant through Paris, measured from Barcelona to Dunkirk. Napoleon carried the metric system through lands he conquered, and it gained traction across Europe.

segments.title: Early US standards: Jefferson, Jay's Treaty, and Adams
segments.summary: The US federal government recognized the need for uniform measures, placed it in the Constitution, and Thomas Jefferson favored the decimal system but backed off after concerns about trusting the French. Jay's Treaty strained relations with France. John Quincy Adams ordered a survey and the US kept its existing system.

segments.title: 1866 law, Treaty of the Meter, and Mendenhall Order
segments.summary: Andrew Johnson signed a law in 1866 making metric use legal in US contracts but not compulsory. The US was not invited to the 1875 Treaty of the Meter signing, though it later signed. Mendenhall's order defined US units in terms of metric standards, so the customary system is effectively defined by metric.

segments.title: 1960 SI redefinition, 1975 Metric Conversion Act, and modern US use
segments.summary: In 1960 the meter and second were redefined using universal physical constants and the system became the SI. The 1975 Metric Conversion Act made metric the preferred system but kept the transition voluntary. Federal agencies went metric by 1992, while industries such as pharmaceuticals and beverages adopted it to varying degrees. The Mars Climate Orbiter loss is cited as an example of mixed units, and the hosts discuss costs and American resistance.

segments.title: Amy Wang metrica thesis and closing discussion
segments.summary: The hosts mention a listener's design thesis called Metrica, which proposed putting metric units into everyday items. They conclude that the US is largely on the metric system in practice.

segments.title: Listener mail: Anchorage student and Rotary exchange
segments.summary: A listener from Anchorage, Alaska, says the podcast inspired them to join a Rotary study-abroad program for next year. The hosts respond and invite listener feedback on American stubbornness.
